idiom_name: embedding wrapper plus an identity-keyed side table (map/RWMutex, sync.Map) or context.WithValue
implementation_notes: Go cannot add methods or fields to a type declared in another package - a method declaration requires the receiver base type to be defined in the same package - so the behaviour half is expressed either by wrapping: a new struct embeds the original type, the embedded field promotes its methods and the new field/methods carry the extension, or by interfaces: a client declares the interface it needs and any type that happens to have those methods satisfies it without modification (structural typing describes existing behaviour, it cannot add any). The attribute half is a hand-written side table: map[*T]State guarded by a mutex, or sync.Map for the read-mostly case. For attributes that travel with a request, context.WithValue is the idiomatic carrier - keys are unexported types and packages expose typed accessors, and the standard library explicitly scopes values to request-scoped data.
pitfalls: A side table keyed by a pointer holds a strong reference to the key, so every subject stays alive for the life of the map: delete the entry when the subject is released (or key by a stable ID with an explicit Close/finalizer) or the table is a leak.

The wrapper route changes identity: the wrapper is a different value from the original, so code holding the original *T never sees the attached state, and embedding a nil pointer (embedding *T without initialising it) makes every promoted method panic.

context.WithValue keys must be unexported package types (a bare string key collides across packages) and values must be safe for concurrent use; using a context as a general attribute bag is explicitly discouraged by the standard library and hides the dependency from the signature.

There are no zero-cost per-instance attributes in Go: the side table costs a lock per access, and sync.Map is only faster than map+RWMutex for its two intended workloads (grow-only caches, disjoint key sets).
